rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: ❌ The cross product gives a scalar. ✅ The cross product gives a VECTOR. The result is perpendicular to both input vectors. The dot product gives a scalar; the cross product gives a vector.  ·  ❌ $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = \vec{B} \times \vec{A}$. ✅ The cross product is ANTI-COMMUTATIVE: $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = -(\vec{B} \times \vec{A})$. Reversing the order flips the direction by 180°.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: ❌ The cross product is defined for any number of vectors. ✅ The cross product is defined only for EXACTLY TWO vectors in 3D space. You cannot take $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} \times \vec{C}$ without parentheses — it is not associative.  ·  ❌ If $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = 0$, then both $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ must be zero vectors. ✅ If $\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = 0$, then either $\vec{A} = 0$, $\vec{B} = 0$, OR $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ are PARALLEL. Any one of these conditions makes the cross product zero.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: The cross product was independently developed by Josiah Willard Gibbs and Oliver Heaviside in the 1880s as part of their effort to simplify vector calculus for physics applications.  ·  The cross product is unique to three dimensions (and seven dimensions with a special construction). In 3D, it is essential for describing rotation, angular momentum, and magnetic forces.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **Definition:** The cross product (vector product) of two vectors $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ is a vector $\vec{C} = \vec{A} \times \vec{B}$ whose magnitude is $AB\sin\theta$ and whose direction is perpendicular to the plane containing $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$.  ·  **Magnitude:** $|\vec{A} \times \vec{B}| = AB\sin\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the two vectors ($0° \leq \theta \leq 180°$).  ·  **Direction — right-hand rule:** Point the fingers of your right hand in the direction of $\vec{A}$, then curl them toward $\vec{B}$. Your thumb points in the direction of $\vec{A} \times \vec{B}$. The result is a vector perpendicular to both $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Concept 5: Connection between Resolution of Vectors and Unit Vectors and other topics  ·  ❌ The right-hand rule is arbitrary and any convention works. ✅ The right-hand rule is a CONVENTION, but it must be consistent throughout physics. Using the left-hand rule would flip the sign of torque, angular momentum, and magnetic force, causing contradictions.  ·  ❌ $\vec{A} \times (\vec{B} \times \vec{C}) = (\vec{A} \times \vec{B}) \times \vec{C}$. ✅ The cross product is NOT ASSOCIATIVE. In general, $\vec{A} \times (\vec{B} \times \vec{C}) \neq (\vec{A} \times \vec{B}) \times \vec{C}$.…

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ The cross product exists in 2D. ✅ The cross product is defined in 3D (and 7D with special structure). In 2D, you can compute a "pseudo-cross product" that gives a scalar ($A_x B_y - A_y B_x$), but this is not a true vector cross product.  ·  Carefully distinguish between similar-looking concepts in resolution of vectors and unit vectors.  ·  Pay attention to the conditions under which formulas and theorems apply.
